title: Inventory Agreement & Pronouns
description: Edit agreement and pronoun problems without being distracted by nearby nouns.
subject: rla
passage:
At the end of each month, a small electronics shop prepares an inventory report. The report lists items that are running low, equipment that needs repair, and supplies that should be reordered. Because several employees contribute notes, the final draft often contains agreement and pronoun problems that are easy to miss during a quick read.

The store manager reminds the team that the grammatical subject controls the verb even when another noun appears closer to it. Phrases such as “along with the spare cables” or “of the replacement parts” can distract an editor from the true subject. Compound subjects and indefinite pronouns require attention as well because they do not always follow the pattern a reader expects from casual speech.

Pronouns create a different problem. A pronoun must clearly refer to the intended noun, and its form must fit its job in the sentence. If two possible nouns appear before “it” or “they,” the sentence may need to be rewritten rather than merely corrected for number. The team’s goal is simple: a reader should never have to stop and guess who completed an action, which item is being discussed, or whether the verb belongs with a nearby distractor instead of the actual subject.

questions.prompt: The inventory sheet {{blank}} on the service counter.
questions.explanation: The subject 'sheet' is singular, so the singular verb 'is' agrees with it.
questions.rule: Match the verb to the actual subject, not to a nearby noun.

options.whyWrong: 'Sheet' is singular, so the plural verb 'are' does not agree.
'Were' is plural and also shifts the sentence into past tense.
'Have been' is plural and does not match the singular subject 'sheet'.

questions.prompt: Rina labeled the scanner before returning {{blank}} to storage.
questions.explanation: The singular pronoun 'it' clearly refers to the singular noun 'scanner'.
questions.rule: Check both pronoun number and pronoun case.

options.whyWrong: 'Scanner' is singular, so the plural pronoun 'them' does not match.
'Their' is possessive and cannot function as the object of 'returning' here.
'They' is a subject form, but the sentence needs an object after 'returning'.

questions.prompt: The box of replacement cables {{blank}} beside the service counter.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'box,' so 'is' agrees with it.
questions.rule: Cross out interrupting prepositional phrases before matching subject and verb.

options.whyWrong: 'Cables' is inside a prepositional phrase; it is not the subject.
This plural verb phrase does not agree with the singular subject 'box'.
This changes both number and tense without support from the sentence.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest revision: “When Leo placed the tablet beside the charger, it was damaged.”
questions.explanation: Naming the damaged item removes the ambiguous pronoun reference.
questions.rule: If a pronoun could point to two nouns, name the exact noun.

options.text: When Leo placed the tablet beside the charger, it was damaged.
options.whyWrong: 'It' could refer to either the tablet or the charger.

options.text: Leo placed the damaged tablet beside the charger.
When Leo placed it beside it, the damage was visible.
options.whyWrong: Replacing both nouns with pronouns makes the reference even less clear.

options.text: The tablet and charger were beside it when Leo noticed damage.
options.whyWrong: 'It' still lacks a clear antecedent.

questions.prompt: The manager, together with two assistants, {{blank}} the final inventory.
questions.explanation: The true subject is 'manager,' so the singular verb 'reviews' agrees with it.
questions.rule: Ignore together with/as well as phrases when finding the core subject.

options.whyWrong: The phrase 'together with two assistants' does not make the singular subject plural.
This plural verb does not agree with the singular subject 'manager'.
This plural form changes both agreement and tense.

questions.prompt: Each technician should record {{blank}} own inspection notes before leaving.
questions.explanation: Singular 'their' is standard and clearly refers back to 'each technician'.
questions.rule: Keep the pronoun tied to the intended antecedent without changing point of view.

options.whyWrong: 'Our' changes the point of view and does not refer back to 'each technician'.
'Your' changes the sentence to second person.
'Its' normally refers to a thing or organization rather than a person here.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest grammatically correct revision: “The inspection committee, along with two supervisors, review the incident notes before they submits its recommendation.”
questions.explanation: 'Committee' takes the singular verb 'reviews,' and repeating 'the committee' removes the unclear pronoun while keeping 'submits' in agreement with that singular subject.
questions.rule: On dense edits, check agreement first, then confirm every pronoun has one clear antecedent.

options.text: The inspection committee, along with two supervisors, review the incident notes before the committee submits its recommendation.
options.whyWrong: Naming the committee fixes the pronoun reference, but 'committee' still needs the singular verb 'reviews'.

options.text: The inspection committee, along with two supervisors, reviews the incident notes before they submits its recommendation.
options.whyWrong: 'Reviews' agrees with 'committee,' but 'they submits' has a pronoun-verb agreement error and an unclear reference.

options.text: The inspection committee, along with two supervisors, reviews the incident notes before the committee submits its recommendation.
The inspection committee, along with two supervisors, reviews the incident notes before the supervisors submits their recommendation.
options.whyWrong: The final clause shifts the recommendation to the supervisors and also uses the singular verb 'submits' with the plural subject 'supervisors'.

questions.prompt: Choose the best revision: “Neither of the warehouse teams have finished its count, so the manager asked it to submit their totals by noon.”
questions.explanation: 'Neither' agrees with the singular verb 'has,' and 'each team ... its total' keeps the later pronoun reference and number agreement clear.
questions.rule: A revision can fix the first agreement error and still fail later pronoun agreement—check the whole sentence.

options.text: Neither of the warehouse teams have finished their count, so the manager asked each team to submit its total by noon.
options.whyWrong: The pronoun reference is clearer, but 'neither' still requires the singular verb 'has'.

options.text: Neither of the warehouse teams has finished its count, so the manager asked it to submit its total by noon.
options.whyWrong: 'Has' agrees with 'neither,' but the later 'it' can ambiguously refer to one team rather than clearly applying the request to each team.

options.text: Neither of the warehouse teams has finished their count, so the manager asked them to submit its total by noon.
options.whyWrong: The sentence mixes plural and singular pronouns, so the reference and number relationship are inconsistent.

options.text: Neither of the warehouse teams has finished its count, so the manager asked each team to submit its total by noon.

curriculum.learningObjective: Edit agreement and pronoun problems without being distracted by nearby nouns.
